cells.tense: You are here with the pen and the compass inside you reading clear.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: Take one thing that ended in the past year and write down three things it left behind that you still use—then stop the count and put the page away.
cells.core:
Your private compass is reading clear. You can feel what's fair in a situation without running it through a machine, and that reading doesn't fight the pull toward what's ahead. The weight you carry feels accurate and not heavy. You know what you owe and what you're owed, and the reading doesn't grip.

What this balance can feed next is the harvest: the yield of a slow season, sitting there unpicked. Take something that ended in the past year—a job, a relationship that changed shape, a long recovery—and count what it actually left behind. Three things you still use. Not lessons, not silver linings, just what stayed. Write them once and put the page where you'll see it. The harvest is quiet, and it's yours to take in.
cells.sheetLine: The season grew something in you
cells.verb: Weighing what is fair by an inner sense, a private compass reading true.
cells.place: An inspired orientation toward a light that is recognized, not arrived at.

cells.tense: You will be auditing a future that hasn't arrived, checking its fairness before it lands.
cells.act: hold someone else up with what you have
cells.ask: Pick one person near you carrying a heavy week, and take one whole task off their hands—something you can finish alone—then hand it back and step away.
cells.core:
The bracing is real: you're already weighing a future that hasn't happened, checking exchanges before they occur. The compass that usually reads quiet has turned into a guard, and leaving something unresolved feels like a debt. There's tightness in it. The pull toward light is still there, and a need to settle the whole account in advance keeps squeezing it.

What's thin isn't restraint, it's contact. Find one person near you who's carrying a heavy week, and take one whole task off their hands—something you can finish alone, not advice, not a plan. Hand it back and step away. Doing one real thing in the present gives the compass a present to read instead of a future to audit. One finished act is all this needs, and then you stop.

cells.tense: You were standing at a door that had already closed behind you, looking back.
cells.act: walk the route with someone who is lost on it
cells.ask: Go along with one person who is stuck where you once were. Stay for the first stretch, then turn back and let them keep the rest of the walk alone.
cells.core:
Something you used to feel sure about got left at a threshold you didn't notice closing. The direction forward feels like a memory instead of a pull, and the aim you once trusted has gone quiet. You're holding a position that no longer exists, and that's why forward is hard to feel. The under-expression isn't laziness; your energy is going into a room you've already left.

Direction comes back by being handed out rather than found again. Find one person stuck where you once stood—a job, a move, a choice you've made—and walk the first stretch with them. First week, first call, first draft. Stay long enough to be useful, then turn back and leave the rest of the road to them. Escorting someone a little way returns your own footing to you, and this one ends when you turn back.

cells.tense: You are holding the pen and calling the writing someone else's hand.
cells.act: sort the kinds of pull from one another
cells.ask: Take what is pulling at you this week and put it into three piles—what you owe, what others want, what you actually want—then leave the piles where you can see them.
cells.core:
You can feel when an exchange is off—there's a drag in your chest near it—and you can feel when something is right. The compass is working. What's missing is your name on it. You talk about fairness the way you'd describe a season, as something that happens to you rather than something you're steering. The pull toward light is real, and you've been calling it someone else's idea.

Sorting the pulls is the act. Put this week's tugging into three piles: what you owe, what others want from you, and what you actually want. Some will be clean; some will carry fingerprints. Don't fix anything. Just sort them onto the page and leave them there. The sorting puts the pen back in your hand, and you'll know it by the quiet that follows.
